title: Callbacks, promises and async/await
summary: From error-first callbacks to promises and async functions, running work in sequence or in parallel, and the combinators you reach for every day.

sections.title: Error-first callbacks
sections.body:
Classic Node APIs take a callback as the last argument and call it as `callback(err, result)`. If `err` is not null, `result` must be ignored. Two rules keep callback code safe: always return after handling an error, and never call the callback twice.

`util.promisify` wraps any function that follows this convention and returns a promise-based version; most built-ins also ship promise APIs directly, such as `node:fs/promises`.

sections.title: Promises and async functions
sections.body:
A promise is a placeholder for a value that settles once: **fulfilled** or **rejected**. `then` returns a new promise, so chains pass values along and a rejection skips ahead to the next `catch`.

An `async` function always returns a promise. `await` pauses the function until the promise settles and either gives you the value or throws the rejection, so plain `try`/`catch`/`finally` handles async errors. `await` only pauses that function, never the thread.

sections.title: Sequential versus parallel
sections.body:
`await` in a loop runs one item at a time. When the items are independent, start them all and wait once:

- `Promise.all` resolves with every result in order and rejects as soon as **one** rejects (the others keep running; their results are ignored).
- `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and reports each `{status, value | reason}`.
- `Promise.race` settles with the first to settle; `Promise.any` resolves with the first to **fulfill** and rejects only if all reject (`AggregateError`).

For hundreds of items, unbounded parallelism can exhaust sockets or hit rate limits; run them through a pool with a fixed concurrency instead.

sections.title: Cancellation with AbortController
sections.body:
Promises cannot be cancelled by themselves. The platform answer is an `AbortSignal`: the caller creates an `AbortController`, passes `controller.signal` down, and calls `controller.abort(reason)` later. `fetch`, timers in `node:timers/promises`, streams and many fs calls accept a `signal`.

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives a signal that aborts on its own, and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` combines signals. In your own functions, check `signal.aborted` before starting and listen for the `'abort'` event while waiting.

pitfalls: Forgetting `await`, so errors escape the surrounding `try`.
Using `await` in a loop for independent work and making it serial.
`forEach` with an async callback: nothing waits for the callbacks.
Calling a callback twice, for example once in the error path and again after it.

gotchas.question: Why does `items.forEach(async x => await save(x))` not wait?
gotchas.answer: `forEach` ignores the promises that the async callback returns, so the surrounding code continues immediately and rejections become unhandled. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential work or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))` for parallel work.

gotchas.question: What is the difference between `return promise` and `return await promise` inside `try`?
gotchas.answer: With `return await`, a rejection is thrown inside the `try`, so the `catch` and the stack trace include this function. With a bare `return`, the promise is handed back unawaited and the local `catch` never runs.

gotchas.question: `Promise.all` rejected. Did the other tasks stop?
gotchas.answer: No. Promises are not cancellable, so the other operations keep running and their results are dropped. To actually stop them, pass an `AbortSignal` and abort it when one fails.
